justification_text:
The point estimates reflect the central value I expect the variable of interest to be at each time horizon (1 day, 1 week, and 1 month). These estimates are steady across all horizons (136.18) because they likely represent either a baseline or an underlying trend based on historical patterns or known drivers of behavior in the system. In the short term, minimal changes are expected, barring any impactful, unforeseen events, and over longer horizons, the point estimate implicitly assumes that the fundamental drivers of the system (such as current trends, external conditions, or other factors) will remain consistent or revert to the expected mean.

The width of the confidence intervals captures the significant sources of uncertainty that grow as the forecast horizon increases. Over one day, uncertainties are small because most influencing factors—whether market forces, natural patterns, or other dynamics—are relatively stable and predictable in such a short time frame. Over one week, the uncertainty widens significantly, because more time allows for small deviations to accumulate or for medium-sized, unexpected events to have an impact. By the one-month horizon, the confidence interval becomes substantially wider. This reflects the understanding that dynamic systems are harder to forecast as the influence of randomness, noise, or structural shifts compounds with time. Factors such as market volatility, weather variability, changes in public sentiment, unexpected supply or demand shocks, or even geopolitical events might contribute to this widening uncertainty.

Specific risks or events could still push outcomes outside the stated intervals, even though those intervals are designed to cover 90% of plausible outcomes. Significant "black swan" events—such as a global financial crisis, a large-scale natural disaster, or sudden policy changes—could create shocks well beyond the modeled uncertainty. Similarly, major shifts in correlated drivers—for instance, a sudden and unexpected market correction, regulatory intervention, or breakthrough innovation—might rapidly realign the system in ways not entirely captured by the historical data or assumptions used in the forecast model. While rare, these tail risks are a reminder that even confident predictions can't account for every possible scenario.
